planting.note: Sow directly in early spring, and again in late summer where summers are mild, harvesting outer leaves as they size up.

directions: Sow directly in early spring, and again in late summer where summers are mild, harvesting outer leaves as they size up for extended cut-and-come-again production. An Australian heirloom loose-leaf lettuce with tall, crinkled, chartreuse-yellow leaves and notable heat tolerance, it is a reliable performer where many lettuces bolt or turn bitter in warm weather. It has been preserved largely through heirloom seed exchanges as a distinct warm-climate alternative to common green and red leaf types.

planting.note: Sow directly in early spring and successively every few weeks for a steady supply of tender young leaves.

directions: Sow directly in early spring and successively every few weeks for a steady supply of tender young leaves, since older leaves and stems toughen as plants approach flowering. This golden-yellow-leaved form of mountain spinach has been grown as a spinach substitute since antiquity and tolerates heat and poor soil far better than true spinach, eventually bolting to tall, ornamental seed spikes in summer. Its bright color makes it a popular contrast alongside the more familiar red and green orach forms in mixed salad plantings.

planting.note: Sow directly in spring for a quick cutting crop or in late summer for a fall and early-winter harvest, cutting leaves at the base to encourage regrowth.

directions: Sow directly in spring for a quick cutting crop or in late summer for a fall and early-winter harvest, cutting leaves at the base to encourage regrowth. An Italian dandelion-leaf chicory of the Catalogna group, with long, smooth, sword-shaped serrated leaves and a mildly bitter, herbaceous flavor best known cooked but also usable young in salads. It has long been a staple green in southern Italian cooking, traditionally sautéed with garlic and olive oil.

planting.note: Sow in mid-to-late summer for a fall and early-winter harvest, since it tolerates light frost and even improves in flavor after cool weather.

directions: Sow in mid-to-late summer for a fall and early-winter harvest, since it tolerates light frost and even improves in flavor after cool weather, or sow in early spring for a summer crop. A French heirloom frisée-type endive named for the town of Ruffec, it is prized for its finely dissected, deeply curled dark-green leaves and notable cold hardiness compared to other curly endives. Traditionally the outer leaves are gathered and tied to blanch the heart, producing the pale, tender center prized in French bistro salads.
